extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and social/scientific method; readers of political and social theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative standards for constructing and testing theories in psychology, ethology, and the social sciences, including when to use deduction vs. induction and the limits of experimental/comparative methods. Emphasizes verification, consilience of a priori and a posteriori evidence, and the proper relation between science and applied art (policy/education).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositions afterward recognized as the most general truths of the science were, of all its accurate generalizations, those earliest arrived at (example: laws of motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume it is vicious to 'fly to the highest generalizations first'; the real error is making large generalizations without rigorous inductive warrant and applying them deductively without verification. Where rigorous induction is possible, obtaining the highest (most general) truths first can be both usual and desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain truths where real induction is most realizable
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain those first in respect to which the conditions of a real induction can be first and most completely realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simplest cases (fewest causes simultaneously concerned) because they are most amenable to induction and often elicit laws of greatest comprehensiveness. Seek situations where causes are reachable rather than stopping at empirical laws of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification must accompany deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The inference given by theory as to the type of character which would be formed by any given circumstances must be tested by specific experience of those circumstances whenever obtainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction a priori; theory cannot be trusted unless confirmed by observation, nor observation unless affiliated to theory. Aim for consilience between a priori reasoning and specific experience as the sufficient ground for principles in complex sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethology as a deductive science founded on psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethology, the deductive science, is a system of corollaries from Psychology, the experimental science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction of Ethology requires deducing ethological consequences from psychological laws and verifying those deductions against empirical laws formed by observation and history. The science’s progress depends on both theoretical deduction and detailed empirical study of human types and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part method for creating Ethology
rubrics_metrics.description: The progress of this important but most imperfect science will depend on a double process: first, deducing theoretically the ethological consequences of particular circumstances; and, secondly, the reverse operation—increased study of various types of human nature combined with psychological explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical study must be conducted by observers who can analyze circumstances and apply psychological laws to explain characteristics; residual unexplained differences may be attributed to congenital predispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective standard for a successful social science
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of society would have attained a very high point of perfection if it enabled us ... to understand by what causes [a society] had been made what it was; whether it was tending to any, and to what, changes; what effects each feature of its existing state was likely to produce; and by what means any of those effects might be prevented, modified, or accelerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social-science theories by their ability to (1) explain historical causes, (2) diagnose tendencies, (3) predict likely consequences of features, and (4) indicate practical means for altering those consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science should prepare but not replace art (policy/practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A science which possesses middle principles ... is duly prepared to be the foundation of the corresponding Art. Practical education will be the mere transformation of those principles into a parallel system of precepts, adapted to individual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect universal precepts from social science; the art (policy, education) must adapt scientific middle principles to particular cases, watching circumstances and tailoring measures to desired effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes in social phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In social phenomena the Composition of Causes is the universal law: human beings in society have no properties but those derived from the laws of individual human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating societies as substances with novel properties independent of individuals. Analyze social effects as composed results of individual-level causes and their interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of experimental ('chemical') method in social science
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of philosophizing which may be termed chemical overlooks that the nature of man as an individual is concerned, and proceeds as if specific experience alone could determine political truths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of drawing general political conclusions from single historical instances or unanalysed comparisons (e.g., 'England has flourished under X, therefore X is good'). Controlled experiments are impossible for nations; the chemical method therefore yields arguments that would not be accepted in experimental sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure of Method of Difference for social causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply the Method of Difference we require instances which tally in every particular except the one which is the subject of inquiry; such an experimentum crucis is impossible for nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat cross-national comparisons as conclusive unless you can plausibly show all other antecedents are the same—an unrealistic standard. Recognize that differences in legislation reflect deeper differences in position, interests, opinions, habits, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Indirect Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparing one nation with two others that 'agree in nothing but' a given circumstance still fails because national prosperity is the collective result of a multitude of favorable circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring causation from class comparisons that ignore many interacting favorable/unfavorable conditions; prosperity may arise from the aggregate of causes, not any single one isolated by crude classing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement and Concomitant Variations inadequate under plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement is of little value in cases admitting plurality of causes; elimination of antecedents doesn't prove a single antecedent is the cause when multiple causes may combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer that an antecedent which cannot be eliminated is therefore the unique cause. Concomitant variation is unreliable when many co‑operating causes affect the same aggregate attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues presupposes deductive knowledge of some causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Residues concludes, after allowing for effects of known causes, that the unexplained residue may be imputed to remaining circumstances; it presupposes that those known causes are already known by deduction from principles of human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat empirical residue-analysis as supplementing, not replacing, deduction. Because specific experience cannot on its own establish the many underlying causes, deduction from general laws is necessary to identify components before subtracting them from observed effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of integrating deduction and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The experimental argument amounts to anything only in verification of a conclusion drawn from those general laws; we may subtract the effect of some causes but never of all except one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical observations chiefly to verify and refine deductions from laws of human nature; avoid attempting to base political science solely on inductive enumeration of historical instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the geometrical/abstract method as a model without modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Some thinkers assimilate deductive social science to geometry; but geometry is a science of co-existent facts and affords no room for conflicting causes as occur in social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the social sciences must be deductive in large part, do not model them on geometry's form. Account explicitly for conflicting and counteracting causes (like forces in mechanics) when constructing deductive arguments about social phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of historical analogies as decisive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from historical examples (Athens or Rome, fires in Smithfield, the French Revolution) that draw universal precepts are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical analogies can be suggestive but are not substitutes for systematic deduction from human-nature laws plus careful verification; avoid deriving universal policy maxims from isolated historical parallels.
